refs.quote: Common adverse reactions to systemically administered epinephrine include anxiety, apprehensiveness, restlessness, tremor, weakness, dizziness, sweating, palpitations, pallor, nausea and vomiting, headache, and respiratory difficulties.

value: Injection site necrosis / necrotizing fasciitis (rare IM thigh)

refs.quote: Overdosage of epinephrine may produce extremely elevated arterial pressure, which may result in cerebrovascular hemorrhage, particularly in elderly patients. Overdosage may also result in pulmonary edema because of peripheral vascular constriction together with cardiac stimulation.

Rare cases of serious skin and soft tissue infections, including necrotizing fasciitis and myonecrosis caused by Clostridia (gas gangrene), have been reported following epinephrine injection in the thigh [ see Warnings and Precautions (5.2) ].

mechanism_of_action.value: Epinephrine acts on both alpha and beta-adrenergic receptors, increasing ventricular contractility (positive inotropic), heart rate (positive chronotropic), and peripheral vasoconstriction.

refs.quote: Epinephrine acts on both alpha and beta-adrenergic receptors. The mechanism of the rise in blood pressure is 3-fold: a direct myocardial stimulation that increases the strength of ventricular contraction (positive inotropic action), an increased heart rate (positive chronotropic action), and peripheral vasoconstriction.

Following intravenous injection, epinephrine is rapidly cleared from the plasma with an effective half-life of < 5 minutes. A pharmacokinetic steady state following continuous intravenous infusion is achieved within 10 to 15 minutes.

value.effect: Potentiates cardiovascular pressor and arrhythmogenic effects of epinephrine.
value.management: Monitor blood pressure and ECG continuously; start at lower infusion rates.

refs.quote: Drugs that potentiate the effects of epinephrine include sympathomimetics, beta blockers, tricyclic antidepressants, MAO inhibitors, COMT inhibitors, clonidine, doxapram, oxytocin, levothyroxine sodium, quinidine and certain antihistamines.

value.effect: Unopposed alpha-adrenergic vasoconstriction can cause severe hypertension and reflex bradycardia.
value.management: Monitor arterial blood pressure closely; consider alternative pressor/vasodilator strategies.

refs.quote: Drugs that potentiate the effects of epinephrine include sympathomimetics, beta blockers, tricyclic antidepressants, MAO inhibitors, COMT inhibitors, clonidine, doxapram, oxytocin, levothyroxine sodium, quinidine and certain antihistamines.
Drugs that counter the pressor effects of epinephrine include alpha blockers, vasodilators such as nitrates, diuretics, antihypertensives and ergot alkaloids.

tier.note: 5-axis synthesis: Prolonged human experience has not identified increased major birth defects, though label notes potential fetal harm from uterine vasoconstriction/hypoxia; in maternal anaphylaxis or shock, epinephrine must not be withheld.

refs.quote: Prolonged experience with epinephrine use in pregnant women over several decades, based on published literature, do not identify a drug associated risk of major birth defects, miscarriage or adverse maternal or fetal outcomes.

In pregnant patients with septic, cardiogenic, or anaphylactic shock, maternal hemodynamic stabilization and restoration of uteroplacental perfusion take absolute priority; norepinephrine and epinephrine should not be withheld due to theoretical fetal concerns.

pregnancy_pk.value: No formal pregnancy PK dose adjustment; titrate to lowest effective dose for maternal MAP/anaphylaxis reversal with continuous fetal monitoring.

refs.quote: Because alpha-adrenergic vasoconstriction can reduce uterine blood flow, titrate to the lowest effective dose with continuous fetal heart rate monitoring when viable. lactation_rid.value: Not established (expected negligible oral infant absorption)

refs.quote: No data are available on the excretion of epinephrine into human milk.

lactation_summary.value: Poor oral bioavailability and plasma half-life < 5 minutes make clinically significant infant exposure via breastmilk unlikely.

refs.quote: There is no information regarding the presence of epinephrine in human milk or the effects of epinephrine on the breastfed infant or on milk production. However, due to its poor oral bioavailability and short half-life, epinephrine exposure is expected to be very low in the breastfed infant.

Because epinephrine is poorly absorbed orally and rapidly inactivated in the infant gastrointestinal tract, maternal intravenous or parenteral administration is not expected to cause adverse effects in breastfed infants.
